items.title: Stay up to date with regulatory compliance at the FAAA Congress
items.teaser: The upcoming Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) Congress will explore ASIC's key focus for the remainder of the year, while shedding some light on the ongoing developments from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) and the Compensation Scheme as Last Resort (CSLR).
items.brief_text: The upcoming Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) Congress will explore ASIC's key focus for the remainder of the year, while shedding some light on the ongoing developments from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) and the Compensation Scheme as Last Resort (CSLR). This year's congress, themed 'EXPLORE,' reflects the core purpose to providing financial advisers with the opportunity to explore new ideas, practical strategies and industry developments that help to better serve their clients, the FAAA said. "It's also about exploring different perspectives through conversations with peers, experts and industry leaders, and taking away insights that can be applied immediately in their businesses," the association said. Participating in two separate panels, FAAA general manager of policy, advocacy and standards Phil Anderson, noted attendees can expect what the regulator is bringing to the table in relation to the Delivering Better Financial Outcomes (DBFO) reforms, the CSLR, as well as other announcements from assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino last month , in a discussion between himself, ASIC senior executive leader Leah Sciacca, and FAAA policy and advocacy consultant Andrea Forbes. "We certainly expect to see an answer on the CSLR special levy," Anderson said. "We expect to see some more progress on the education standards, and we'll also talk about the reform on AML/CTF and how it impacts advisers.

items.title: Auditor suspended over three Australian Fiduciaries audits
items.teaser: Cameron Bradley, formerly a partner of PKF Brisbane Audit, will be suspended until 30 June 2028, according to ASIC. The regulator said the CADB’s determination was based on the fact Bradley has voluntarily stepped down as a registered company auditor on 1 July 2025.
items.brief_text: Cameron Bradley, formerly a partner of PKF Brisbane Audit, will be suspended until 30 June 2028, according to ASIC. The regulator said the CADB’s determination was based on the fact Bradley has voluntarily stepped down as a registered company auditor on 1 July 2025. The CADB will also require Bradley to give certain undertakings including future peer reviews and additional continuing professional development. Following an investigation, ASIC referred Bradley to the CADB in June 2025 over his conduct in three managed investment scheme audits for the financial year ended 30 June 2023. The schemes included: Global Diversified Alpha Fund, Global All Seasons Fund, and Global Mutli-Strategy Fund. The responsible entity for all three schemes is Australian Fiduciaries Limited. The CADB found Bradley had failed to properly perform his duties as auditor when assessing the schemes’ financial assets, which accounted for more than 90 per cent of their total assets. The schemes sat at the top of a complex, multi-tiered investment structure spanning at least four levels and involving multiple funds and trusts. Ultimately, the underlying assets were properties used as disability accommodation under the NDIS.

items.title: How to classify your SMSF as a wholesale client: A compliance guide for trustees and advisers
items.teaser: AFCA’s view is that, in these circumstances, section 761G(6) requires the SMSF itself to satisfy a $10 million asset threshold. Because AFCA applies this interpretation when determining complaints, the issue has significant practical implications for trustees, advisers and product providers.
items.brief_text: AFCA’s view is that, in these circumstances, section 761G(6) requires the SMSF itself to satisfy a $10 million asset threshold. Because AFCA applies this interpretation when determining complaints, the issue has significant practical implications for trustees, advisers and product providers. Recent AFCA determinations have also demonstrated that an incorrect wholesale classification can itself become an issue in a complaint, particularly where retail client protections have been denied. In a May 2026 determination involving an SMSF that invested in two wholesale-only funds, AFCA found that the SMSF was a retail client and was not eligible to invest in the funds. AFCA ordered the financial firm to pay $258,690 to the SMSF, plus $5,000 in legal costs. The determination demonstrates that wholesale classification can have significant practical consequences where an SMSF is subsequently found to have been a retail client. This guide sets out the relevant tests, how to tell which one applies, the mistake that catches almost everyone, and how we suggest trustees and advisers approach classification in the meantime. The different wholesale client tests – and why most people only know one of them Under the Corporations Act 2001, whether an SMSF can be treated as a wholesale client depends on the particular financial service being provided, the financial product involved and the statutory test being relied upon.

items.title: ATO expectations for checking disqualified trustees or directors
items.teaser: Kellie Grant, Director, SMSF Regulatory Branch for the ATO, said for compliance checks, the auditor is required to conduct on disqualified trustees under section 126K of the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993 (SISA) which dictates specific compliance audit requirements for SMSFs in Australia.
items.brief_text: Kellie Grant, Director, SMSF Regulatory Branch for the ATO, said for compliance checks, the auditor is required to conduct on disqualified trustees under section 126K o f the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993 (SISA) which dictates specific compliance audit requirements for SMSFs in Australia. “While the auditor is still required to obtain a representation from the individual trustees or directors of the corporate trustee that they’re not disqualified, we’ve provided some more guidance on when they should then do an independent verification check,” Grant said. “That should be in situations where the trustee does not provide a representation, or there’s evidence to suggest that the representation might be unreliable, like they’re dipping into their fund’s’ monies, which could indicate that they’re insolvent, or this is the third year in a row you may have lodged an ACR for these for serious contraventions.

items.title: Major compliance shift coming with director IDs
items.teaser: Formica said the change will force advisers to tighten address records, overhaul onboarding processes and prepare clients for a far more rigorous identity‑matching regime, with annual reviews becoming a key trigger point, and where mismatched ASIC–ABRS details could cause issues.
items.brief_text: Formica said the change will force advisers to tighten address records, overhaul onboarding processes and prepare clients for a far more rigorous identity‑matching regime, with annual reviews becoming a key trigger point, and where mismatched ASIC–ABRS details could cause issues. “Director IDs came in November 2021 and introduced the concept of making sure that someone needed to have a director ID before they became a director of a company, “ Formica said. “For us to get the full benefit of the director ID regime, we needed to be able to link the director IDs to the companies of which that person was a director. Without that, we couldn’t get the benefits around phoenixing activity. There are actually changes coming and effective 1 July 2027, we’ll start the process of linking director IDs to the particular companies of which a person is a director.” Formica said presently every person needs to have a director ID before they can become a director of a company, but there is no requirement for directors to give their director ID to the various companies of which they may be a director, nor is there any requirement for directors to give their director ID to ASIC. “ASIC has no spot to store that particular information. Where we’ve got a situation, where the personal details of a director change like their address, typically speaking, we know that we need to give that information to ASIC,” she said.

items.title: Claude for advisers has regulators and competitors on alert
items.teaser: ASIC says it is closely monitoring developments such as the new Claude for financial advisers’ plugin – launched this week – and its potential implications for the Australian market. Incumbent tech vendors are also watching.
items.brief_text: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says it is closely monitoring developments such as Anthropic’s Claude for financial advisers which was announced on 15 September. An ASIC spokesperson tells Professional Planner the regulator is monitoring developments alongside with peer regulators to assess possible implications for the Australian market. The new Claude product is currently available in the US via integrations with technology vendors such as Salesforce and Vanguard. Between clearing regulatory requirements and setting up data centres, among other things, Claude’s new feature may take two years to reach Australia, if it comes at all. That can get even more complicated if it involves super funds, as trustees would have to sign off on member data being shared with other technology services providers. Incumbent Australian tech vendors are also watching the offshore developments closely as a potential threat to the established order emerges. “I still feel it’ll be quite a few years probably before this happens in a meaningful scale. But I do feel it is inevitable at some point that advisers are going to want this capability,” Finura Group joint managing director Peter Worn tells Professional Planner . The benefit of using an LLM such as Claude is considerable, especially for firms currently using many different advice tech systems.

items.title: MDS calls on Treasury to investigate FSC motives
items.teaser: At it’s Shaping Advice Summit in July, the Financial Services Council (FSC) unveiled the Future of Advice Licensing whitepaper where it put forth two potential models to lift funding for ASIC, describing them as a “moderate recalibration” and a “strong inversion” model.
items.brief_text: At it’s Shaping Advice Summit in July, the Financial Services Council (FSC) unveiled the Future of Advice Licensing whitepaper where it put forth two potential models to lift funding for ASIC, describing them as a “moderate recalibration” and a “strong inversion” model. The crux of these proposals is an increase in the fixed license-level levy from $1,500 to $25,000 for Option A, and up to $40,000 for the Option B. Both also included a reduction in the per-adviser levy with a total funding target of $65.2 million, but the significant uplift in licensee costs put plenty of people on offensive. MDS has been among the critics and is now calling on Treasury to look closer at the FSC proposal, suggesting it would force consolidation in the market while allowing the biggest licensees in the profession to actually reduce their costs at the expense of small AFSLs. “Essentially the entire redistribution flows to the 28 licensees at the top. Those licensees, carrying 5,744 advisers or 37.9 per cent of the profession would collectively save in the order of $2.8 million a year under Option A and $9.3 million under Option B,” MDS director and founder Alex Euvrard and head of strategy Ashley Mahadeea said.

items.title: Div 296 no hurdle to SMSF establishments, Class research finds
items.teaser: There’s never been more money in self-managed super funds than there is today, and the rate they’re being created has never been faster.
items.brief_text: More than 52,000 new SMSFs were established in FY26, the highest number ever recorded, according to new analysis by Class. The total number of funds surpassed 680,000, growth of 7.4 per cent on the year, also the highest total on record. Class chief executive Tim Steele says the growth has come despite Division 296 and new limits on residential property borrowing. “Firstly, I would say at a macro level, SMSFs have just had the strongest year on record,” Steele says. “Despite the kind of regulatory backdrop and potentially changes in relation to things like Div 296, SMSFs are more popular than they’ve ever been.” “The themes around control and flexibility, and people taking an interest and being engaged in their super, are already positive things,” Steele says. Steele says the Div 296 tax change has not deterred even younger members who may cross the $3 million threshold over their working lives. “I think it’s a problem they’d love to have,” Steele says. “When someone age 21 enters the workforce and is contributing 12.5 per cent of their super, that beautiful eighth wonder of the world, compound interest, will mean they can grow a material balance over their lifetime. “I just don’t think the potential risk of, at some stage in your life, having more than $3 million in super, is a deterrent.

items.title: Tribunal affirms ASIC ban on advisers at the centre of Shield and First Guardian failed advice
items.teaser: The Administrative Review Tribunal has affirmed the five-year bans imposed by ASIC on financial advisers Andrew Hanley and Shane Monte Silva for their role in switching clients’ superannuation to Shield and First Guardian without proper assessment.
items.brief_text: The five-year ban imposed by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission on former Venture Egg financial adviser Andrew Hanley and FSGA adviser Shane Monte Silva has been confirmed by the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) on 7 September. In December 2025, ASIC banned Monte Silva for contravening financial services laws when advising five clients to move their superannuation. The five-year ban, which prevents him from providing financial services, was publicly announced in April 2026. Monte Silva applied for a review with the ART. “The Applicant’s conduct has damaged the public’s confidence in, and the integrity of, the financial market relating to superannuation,” the ART said. “He engaged in misleading and deceptive conduct and continued to participate in an advice-giving model despite knowing that it was flawed. “A reasonable and competent financial adviser would have stepped aside and stopped giving the flawed advice. His failure to do so demonstrated a disregard for the law and compliance with regulations.” The decision was based on advice provided by Monte Silva between July and August 2023 to roll their existing superannuation into platforms with substantial investments in Shield and First Guardian. The ART found he was not involved in gathering client information, had limited time to assess client’s circumstances and relied on information provided by others.

items.title: Victims’ advocate says Crole banning ‘best thing ASIC has done’
items.teaser: A leading advocate for investors in the collapsed Shield and First Guardian master funds has welcomed the banning of the former chief executive of the licensee at the centre of investor losses.
items.brief_text: Shield and First Guardian victims’ advocate Melinda Kee says the 10-year ban of former InterPrac managing director Garry Crole, announced by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission on Tuesday, is “one of the best things I think ASIC has done”. ASIC has banned Crole, who stepped down as Sequoia Financial Group chief executive on 22 July but remains a substantial shareholder in the beleaguered ASX-listed wealth management group, from performing, as a director or responsible manager, any function involved in carrying on a financial services business. ASIC said it found that Crole was not a fit and proper person, was not competent, and lacked the diligence and judgement required to perform one or more functions as an officer of an entity carrying on a financial services business. It said InterPrac authorised representatives Venture Egg and Rhys Reilly advised thousands of clients to invest their superannuation in the First Guardian and Shield master funds, which both subsequently collapsed. It found that Crole was “aware of serious concerns regarding the representatives’ financial advice model, which included the use of lead generators, and failed to adequately respond to these concerns”. ASIC also found that Crole did not take adequate care in the management and oversight of InterPrac’s approved product list, which included First Guardian and Shield. “They hit the nail on the head. They absolutely hit the nail on the head,” Kee tells Professional Planner .

items.title: ASIC extends wholesale markets pact with FMSB
items.teaser: ASIC has extended its cooperation with the Financial Markets Standards Board (FMSB) for another three years, continuing a partnership focused on the development of global standards for fair and effective wholesale financing markets.
items.brief_text: ASIC has extended its cooperation with the Financial Markets Standards Board (FMSB) for another three years, continuing a partnership focused on the development of global standards for fair and effective wholesale financing markets. The extension will take the agreement between ASIC and the FMSB through to 25 September 2029, building on an arrangement first established in September 2022 and previously extended in 2024. The agreement provides for FMSB to consult ASIC as it develops draft standards, guidance materials and other publications, while also providing the regulator with periodic updates on the standards body's strategy. ASIC said the relationship reflects the organisation's shared interest in maintaining and, where appropriate, improving best practice standards and operational practices among market intermediaries in Australia. The relationship has also strengthened alongside what ASIC described as an increased Australian connection with the FMSB's board of directors. The extension reinforces ASIC's participation in the development of global industry standards and its engagement with the FMSB on wholesale financial market practices, particularly across fixed income, currencies and commodities markets. However, ASIC's involvement does not amount to an endorsement of FMSB publications. ASIC also stressed that industry standards developed by FMSB do not replace obligations imposed under Australian law.

items.title: MDS drags Treasury to assess FSC levy proposal
items.teaser: My Dealer Services (MDS) has called on Treasury to assess the Financial Services Council's (FSC) latest proposal to lift levies paid by licensees to ASIC, which it describes as an "attack" on small licensees.
items.brief_text: My Dealer Services (MDS) has called on Treasury to assess the Financial Services Council's (FSC) latest proposal to lift levies paid by licensees to ASIC, which it describes as an "attack" on small licensees. MDS has written to the Treasury to intervene, noting that rather than a funding reform, the FSC's motive is to force consolidation of smaller licensees. In its white paper proposal, the FSC recommends redesigning the ASIC financial advice levy to fund supervisory uplift, by materially increasing the licence-level component while reducing the per-adviser burden. Under the first option, it proposes increasing the levy from $1500 to a minimum of $25,000 while proportionately reducing the per-adviser fee from approximately $2,300 to a maximum of $1,700. "This would better align levy incidence with where risk is managed, recognising that continued increases in per-adviser fees are not sustainable as a means of addressing ongoing regulatory costs," the FSC said. Under a second option, FSC recommends raising levy to $40,000 for licensees and per-adviser levy to reduce to $500. MDS noted under this proposal a single adviser practice would face an increase of roughly 600% under the first option and over 950% under the second, while a 300-adviser licensee's levy would fall by around 23%. "Essentially the entire redistribution flows to the 28 licensees at the top.

items.title: Named, but not accused: ASIC’s warning that isn’t a warning
items.teaser: When ASIC warns consumers to take care when dealing with a service provider but doesn’t explain to them why, it does not support informed decision-making. The information published should be sufficiently precise to let the reader understand what is known and what is not and why the warning has been issued.
items.brief_text: Imagine that your business appears on a consumer warning page published by ASIC. The page tells consumers to exercise “additional caution”. It sits within a regulatory campaign prompted by concerns that Australians are being pressured into switching their superannuation and exposed to significant losses. ASIC announces your inclusion in a media release and says it is putting industry participants “on notice”. But ASIC also says that naming your business should not be understood as indicating that any law has been broken, or even as reflecting upon you. What, then, is the public supposed to make of your name being on this list? That is the unresolved contradiction at the centre of ASIC’s list of businesses involved in superannuation lead generation. The List ASIC began publishing ‘the list’ in February 2026 as part of a review of advice licensees using lead-generation services. It initially named 44 entities and added another 19 in June. The list includes lead generators and referral partners, as well as advice licensees, corporate authorised representatives and financial advisers that have acquired leads since 1 July 2024. ASIC says some lead-generation practices may expose consumers to significant losses. Its accompanying warnings refer to high-pressure tactics, “free” superannuation health checks, claims that existing funds are underperforming, limited contact with an adviser, poor product disclosure and promises of unrealistic returns.

items.title: Mirvac appoints funds management CEO
items.teaser: Property fund manager Mirvac has promoted a portfolio manager as its new chief executive for funds management. Effective from 6 October, Kit Georgeos will lead Mirvac’s fund management arm which includes wholesale investment vehicles, capital partnerships and investor relationships.
items.brief_text: Property fund manager Mirvac has promoted a portfolio manager as its new chief executive for funds management. Effective from 6 October, Kit Georgeos will lead Mirvac’s fund management arm which includes wholesale investment vehicles, capital partnerships and investor relationships. She will report to group chief executive Campbell Hanan and join the executive leadership team. Georgeos joined Mirvac in 2023 as fund manager of its Mirvac Wholesale Office Fund and the firm said it will seek a replacement for her on the fund. Prior to joining Mirvac, Georgeos was a fund manager on the AMP Capital Wholesale Office Fund for three years and spent seven years at GPT Group, including two as head of product development. Hanan said: “Kit is an outstanding leader with deep experience across real estate investment, funds management and capital markets, and I am delighted to welcome her to Mirvac’s executive leadership team. “She has built strong investor relationships, demonstrated a disciplined investment approach and shown a clear commitment to delivering long-term outcomes for our capital partners. “Funds management is a core pillar of Mirvac’s strategy and a key driver of our future growth.

items.title: UniSuper hires former TesltraSuper's head of retirement
items.teaser: The super fund has appointed a former TelstraSuper executive to lead its advice strategy, research governance and technical frameworks.
items.brief_text: The super fund has appointed a former TelstraSuper executive to lead its advice strategy, research governance and technical frameworks. Melanie Slade has joined UniSuper as head of advice strategy and technical, reporting to chief advice officer Andrew Gregory, who was previously the head of advice until he was promoted to his current role in September last year . Slade brings over 20 years' experience in financial services, beginning as a financial planner earlier in her career before taking on the role of team leader in financial education and advice team at Superpartners for two years. She was a team manager for advice and engagement at First State Super from 2011 to 2015 and joined TelstraSuper in the same year, serving in various leadership positions, including heading its retirement, product, and member services divisions. TelstraSuper merged with Aware Super in May , some nine months after it first announced that the two funds were exploring a potential merger . Meanwhile, UniSuper said the fund is "incredibly pleased" to welcome Slade and explained that she will lead various "important" initiatives in her new role. "Mel will lead advice strategy, research governance and technical frameworks for UniSuper's advice business, helping shape the future of advice delivery and retirement outcomes for members," a UniSuper spokesperson explained.

items.title: Netwealth to Acquire Paradino
items.teaser: Technology and super platform, Netwealth has announced it will acquire AI automation and productivity platform, Paradino.
items.brief_text: Technology and super platform, Netwealth has announced it will acquire AI automation and productivity platform, Paradino. A message released by Netwealth CEO and Joint MD, Matt Heine, says the joint mission of the two firms is to provide advisers with the tools to automate and streamline their advice process enabling them to scale, drive efficiency

items.title: PPS Mutual appoints new manager to grow presence in Victoria
items.teaser: PPS said her appointment will expand the firm’s reach “at a time when the complexity and cost of Australia’s financial advice framework continues to influence how advisers operate and clients access quality advice – a trend that has seen adviser numbers tighten across the industry, even as demand for specialist…
items.brief_text: PPS said her appointment will expand the firm’s reach “at a time when the complexity and cost of Australia’s financial advice framework continues to influence how advisers operate and clients access quality advice – a trend that has seen adviser numbers tighten across the industry, even as demand for specialist protection advice grows”. Makris will take the on the role of senior business development manager for Victoria, reporting to state manager for Victoria. In this role, she will work towards growing the risk specialist’s presence in Victoria, working with PPS Mutual’s accredited adviser network to strengthen risk insurance capability, supporting sustainable practice development and “help advisers deliver high-quality protection outcomes for professional clients”. Voula brings more than three decades of financial services experience across business development, adviser relationships, distribution and client service. She joins PPS Mutual from Acenda, where she was business development manager, and previously held senior distribution roles at iExtend and Integrity Life. Her career also includes almost 12 years as a business development manager at CommInsure, along with earlier roles at Colonial First State and AMP. PPS Mutual Victoria state manager Shadia Kouzma said the appointment was about more than expanding the insurer’s distribution capability, with a focus on supporting a strong and sustainable risk advice profession.

items.title: Sodor Capital plots New Zealand expansion with new hire
items.teaser: Australian fund distributor Sodor Capital has appointed an executive to lead its New Zealand expansion, while opening a new office in Singapore.
items.brief_text: Australian fund distributor Sodor Capital has appointed an executive to lead its New Zealand expansion, while opening a new office in Singapore. The expansion across the Asia Pacific region follows a distribution mandate awarded to the firm from a European asset manager in March . Sam Dixon has joined Sodor Capital as head of New Zealand, joining from Murray & Co where he was the head of fund distribution for close to three years. He brings 25 years' experience in investment banking and fund management with J.P. Morgan and HSBC across London, Hong Kong , and Sydney. He is also a member of the Institute of Directors in New Zealand and chairs the New Zealand Shareholders Association. Dixon's appointment extends Sodor Capital's distribution reach to connect New Zealand's wholesale and institutional investors with Sodor Capital's distributed funds, simultaneously providing Kiwi fund managers a route to expand their network. Meanwhile, the company has announced the incorporation of Sodor Capital Pte. Ltd in Singapore, establishing a registered presence in the country in building out the firm's longer-term plans in the Southeast Asia. The firm is currently undergoing an extensive recruitment process to support the initiative, it said. Sodor Capital chief executive Martin Smith described both locations are "natural extensions" of the business built in Australia. "This move is about providing our clients with broader regional coverage across Asia Pacific," Smith said.

items.title: Netwealth to acquire AI adviser workflow platform for $29m
items.teaser: According to an ASX announcement, up to a further $9 million in ear-out and retention consideration may also be paid over four years, subject to the satisfaction of agreed outcomes and milestones. Paradino is an AI-enabled advice workflow and automation platform serving financial advisers.
items.brief_text: According to an ASX announcement, up to a further $9 million in ear-out and retention consideration may also be paid over four years, subject to the satisfaction of agreed outcomes and milestones. Paradino is an AI-enabled advice workflow and automation platform serving financial advisers. Its core platform, centred around Athena AI, assists advisers through automation, streamlining the production workflow, including the preparation of documents, client communications, meeting notes and other related administrative activities. The firm currently supports more than 500 financial advisers, generating $1.6 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and integrates with a range of advice technology platforms. Netwealth said that because Paradino is still an early-stage business and had yet to achieve the break-even point, its FY27 earnings before interest, tax, debt and amortisation (EBITDA) is expected to be a loss of $3 million. In order to accelerate the delivery of its product roadmap, Netwealth plans to invest a further $10 million into Paradino over the next two years. “Like Netwealth, Paradino has rapidly gained market support due to its focus on technology, service and innovation, and I’m really pleased to welcome the founders, Alex and Josh, and the whole Paradino team to Netwealth,” Matt Heine, chief executive of Netwealth said.

items.title: The SILC Group names head of trustee
items.teaser: The SILC Group has appointed fund governance executive Kylie Holbrook in the newly created role of head of trustee and responsible entity solutions.
items.brief_text: The SILC Group has appointed fund governance executive Kylie Holbrook in the newly created role of head of trustee and responsible entity solutions. Holbrook will report to Michelle Tay, group executive director, working closely with the leadership team while heading the group's trustee and Responsible Entity teams and associated fund manager relationships. With more than three decades of experience, Holbrook has held senior leadership positions at Perpetual, Equity Trustees and MSC Group. Throughout her career, she has overseen governance frameworks supporting more than $100 billion in funds under management and has developed extensive expertise across regulatory compliance, fiduciary oversight and fund structuring, said the group in a statement. "We are delighted to welcome Kylie to The SILC Group. She brings a wealth of governance experience, deep industry relationships and an exceptional track record. Kylie's expertise aligns strongly with our strategic priorities in the wholesale trustee market and supports the expansion of our recently launched RE business," said Tay. Meanwhile, Kylie Holbrook said she was excited to join the Group at a pivotal time in its growth. "I am delighted to be joining The SILC Group and excited by the opportunity to help take its trustee and Responsible Entity business to the next level," she said.

items.title: Antipodes Partners acquires Bennelong FM
items.teaser: Antipodes Partners will acquire Bennelong Funds Management from Bangarra Group, which includes investment affiliates Quay Global Investors, Bennelong Australian Equity Partners and Skerryvore Asset Management.
items.brief_text: Antipodes Partners will acquire Bennelong Funds Management from Bangarra Group, which includes investment affiliates Quay Global Investors, Bennelong Long Short Equity Management (BLSEM), Bennelong Australian Equity Partners and Skerryvore Asset Management. The acquisition will include Bennelong's distribution partners Allspring Global Investments and Leadenhall Capital Partners. The transaction is expected to complete before the end of September. Antipodes Partners chief executive Andrew Findlay said: "The addition of Bennelong's high-quality investment teams is consistent with our strategy to further diversify the Antipodes platform, broaden our investment offerings and strengthen our distribution capabilities." Bangarra Group founder Jeff Chapman noted as multi-specialist investment firms Bennelong and Antipodes both share a common philosophy and structure. "I am delighted that Antipodes will seek to grow what we have built over twenty years and I wish them every success," Chapman said. The Bennelong investment affiliates will retain investment autonomy, with no changes to their investment personnel, philosophies or strategies as a result of the transaction.

items.title: Esencia Wealth enacts latest NSW advice merger
items.teaser: Esencia Wealth has merged with Generation Wealth Partners, a Sydney advice practice specialising in high-net-worth clients. The merger brings principals Peter Lee and Joe Jutrisa to Esencia Wealth, both joining as partners and senior financial advisers.
items.brief_text: Esencia Wealth has merged with Generation Wealth Partners, a Sydney advice practice specialising in high-net-worth clients. The merger brings principals Peter Lee and Joe Jutrisa to Esencia Wealth, both joining as partners and senior financial advisers. Being part of a larger group will help the pair to focus on spending time with clients while the clients will benefit from more capability, resources and expertise. Generation Wealth has 250 clients which Esencia said will help it towards its goal of 10,000 clients nationwide. Esencia Wealth was formed in the first half of 2024 through the merger of four Sydney-based advice practices: Advise Wise, Insight Private Wealth, Sovereign Wealth Partners, and Randle Advisory. M&A deals since then have included a merger with Cove Financial Group in July , which brought across 650 clients, and FMA Wealth in February , both located in New South Wales. It also enacted a Queensland expansion in early 2026, striking a multi-merger deal with Financial 3 Wealth and Marsden Wealth Advisers, bringing four new financial advisers and around 300 clients to under its domain. Further deals are expected by the end of 2026, chief executive Matthew Fenning said. He said: “Peter and Joe have built a great business based on trust, strong client relationships and a genuine commitment to doing what’s best for their clients. Their values, approach and focus on client outcomes align closely with the culture we are building at Esencia.

items.title: New Retirement Solution helps advisers structure portfolios for longer retirements
items.teaser: Australian Government data shows people aged 65 can expect to live for more than 20 additional years on average so calculating their retirement needs can be difficult.
items.brief_text: Australian Government data shows people aged 65 can expect to live for more than 20 additional years on average so calculating their retirement needs can be difficult. The Russell Retirement Solution includes two new managed portfolios, the Russell Investments Short-Term and Medium-Term Portfolios, alongside a suitable long-term growth portfolio and a purpose-built Retirement Calculator. It allows advisers to structure client assets across three time horizons: near-term spending and liquidity, future income needs and longer-term capital growth. Advisers can use the new Short-Term and Medium-Term Portfolios for the first two horizons, while retaining a suitable existing portfolio for long-term growth. The Retirement Calculator supports implementation and ongoing management of the strategy and helps advisers determine allocations across the three time horizons, models a personalised glide path into retirement and provides guidance to advisers on rebalancing, as client circumstances, spending needs and portfolio balances change. Neil Rogan, Head of Distribution, Australia and New Zealand at Russell Investments, said pre- and post-retirement is not a single investment phase and clients still need long-term growth, but are also drawing from their portfolio to fund their everyday living expenses. “Advisers need a clear way to match client assets to their changing needs. It changes the way advisers need to think about liquidity and investment risk,” Rogan said.

items.title: Akumin wants to support ambitious quality firms
items.teaser: Akumin has welcomed firms with as few as two advisers to more than 100 in 2026, CEO Matt Lawler tells Professional Planner that the licensee’s growth strategy is focused on the ambitions and quality of potential target firms, not their size.
items.brief_text: Akumin has had at least two financial planning businesses join the AFSL in 2026, one with more than 120 advisers and another with just two staff in their financial planning business. Akumin CEO Matt Lawler tells Professional Planner that the licensee’s growth strategy is focused on the ambitions and quality of potential target firms, not their size. “We’re at our best when we’re working with quality firms that have ambitions. [Firms] that want to grow, that are not happy with where they are today, and they’re eager to evolve. That’s probably where we’re at our best,” Lawler says. “And if there are businesses out there that do have ambitions, and that could be to grow, it could be succession planning, it could be to add new services, it could be to increase the number of clients they look after, mergers, acquisitions. We’re well equipped to look after all of those, assist firms with all of those ambitions.” Aperio Financial Services has joined the Akumin AFSL with plans to grow its financial advice services while receiving support from Akumin around recruitment, paraplanning, technology and marketing. Since joining Akumin in February, Aperio has already added one person to its financial planning business, purchased a new Melbourne office, hired five new accounting staff and has plans to add at least another 15 staff to the business.

items.title: Antipodes Partners to acquire Bennelong Funds Management
items.teaser: Pinnacle affiliate Antipodes Partners will acquire 100 per cent of Bennelong Funds Management Group while 4D Infrastructure will join Perennial Partners. Antipodes has now signed a binding agreement with Bangarra Group, the owner of Bennelong.
items.brief_text: Pinnacle affiliate Antipodes Partners will acquire 100 per cent of Bennelong Funds Management Group while 4D Infrastructure will join Perennial Partners. Antipodes has now signed a binding agreement with Bangarra Group, the owner of Bennelong. The transaction is expected to be completed by the end of the month, as it is not subject to regulatory approval. Antipodes is a multi-specialist investment platform comprising five independent investment teams focused on global equities, global credit, global listed infrastructure, Australian value equities and Australian small companies. It manages over $21 billion and was founded in 2015. Andrew Findlay, chief executive of Antipodes Partners, highlights his firm’s diversification strategy as being behind the move. “The addition of Bennelong’s high-quality investment teams is consistent with our strategy to further diversify the Antipodes platform, broaden our investment offerings and strengthen our distribution capabilities.” Scale is also an objective, with John Burke, CEO of Bennelong adding his firm is complementary with Antipodes. “We believe our broad support base of financial advisers and investors will benefit from the combined scale and expertise of both firms.” With the move, Antipodes picks up Bennelong’s investment affiliates including Quay Global Investors, Bennelong Australian Equity Partners and Skerryvore Asset Management.

items.title: Macquarie hit with class action over Shield losses
items.teaser: Last September, Macquarie admitted to contraventions of the Corporations Act related to Shield and agreed to fully compensate impacted members 100 per cent of the amounts they invested, totalling $321 million.
items.brief_text: Last September, Macquarie admitted to contraventions of the Corporations Act related to Shield and agreed to fully compensate impacted members 100 per cent of the amounts they invested, totalling $321 million. Gordon Legal is now alleging that affected investors had not been fully compensated for losses suffered after the collapse. The firm added that investors had also not been compensated for “the growth their superannuation may have achieved if those funds had remained invested elsewhere during that time, or for the distress they have suffered”. Essentially, they are filing for unrealised gains, or ‘but for’ losses which have become a contumacious issue within the CSLR. This follows a March Federal Court ruling that Macquarie had failed to enact proper due diligence in recommending the Shield to investors. At the time, the Court found Macquaire breached the Corps Act after failing to escalate the Shield for closer internal scrutiny, in a case ASIC said underscores trustees’ obligations to actively monitor investment options offered through super platforms. Gordon said the lead applicant (Dessent) has brought forward the class action on behalf of the affected investors and will allege that Macquarie failed to conduct appropriate due diligence and oversight before allowing investments into Shield via its super platform. “The blood just drained from my face when I first saw how my super had dropped,” Dessent said in a Gordon Legal statement. “I was absolutely gutted.

items.title: Taxpayers to foot Age Pension if super turned into ATM: SMC
items.teaser: New modelling by the Super Members Council (SMC) has shown One Nation's superannuation policy could leave taxpayers on the hook to pay up to double the amount taken out.
items.brief_text: New modelling by the Super Members Council (SMC) has shown One Nation's superannuation policy could leave taxpayers on the hook to pay up to double the amount taken out. One Nation is proposing to give Australians paying rent or a mortgage the choice to take one quarter of their future compulsory super contributions as a tax-advantaged 3% pay boost for up to three years. If Australians opt-in to the boost, 9% of their super will still go into their funds, and they can receive 3% of it directly for up to three years. However, research by SMC showed taxpayers would have to fund an extra $14,000 in lifetime Age Pension payments for every median full-time worker aged 25 for three years under One Nation's policy. Additionally, a median full-time worker in the same condition would be $25,000 poorer by retirement. For a couple it would be around $50,000 worse off. "One Nation's policy will not only make Australians poorer and fuel inflation, quickly wiping out the value of any super you withdraw. Now we can see it will also leave taxpayers on the hook for up to double the amount of super that's taken out," SMC chief executive Misha Schubert said. "And that higher bill to taxpayers in Age Pension costs will make it harder to fund the services struggling Australians rely on - hospitals, medicines, schools, roads, and drought and flood relief." Australia is on track to have the lowest pension spending in the OECD, but that trend could be reversed if the policy became law, SMC said.

items.title: Morningstar names APAC investment chief
items.teaser: Morningstar has named James Foot as the chief investment officer for the Asia Pacific (APAC) region, taking over from Matt Wacher after he finished up in the role in May.
items.brief_text: Morningstar has named James Foot as the chief investment officer for the Asia Pacific (APAC) region, taking over from Matt Wacher after he finished up in the role in May. Foot returns to Morningstar after just around two years as the chief investment officer of wealth and private at Commonwealth Bank. He spent close to nine years at Morningstar previously, serving as the head of research for APAC when he left for CBA. "We are delighted to have James rejoin Morningstar. He will work closely with our senior investment leaders including Bryce Anderson, Bianca Rose and Michael Malseed," Morningstar president of research and investments Daniel Needham said. "Supported by the breadth of our Australian and global investment teams, James will play a key role in further strengthening our investment capability and delivering outcomes for clients." Foot said he was excited to return to Morningstar at a pivotal time for investors. "I'm thrilled to be returning to Morningstar and reconnecting with a team that is deeply committed to investor outcomes," Foot said. "As markets become more complex, the combination of rigorous research, disciplined portfolio construction and a long-term perspective have never been more important, and I'm excited to help drive that mission across the region." Needham had assumed the oversight and management of all APAC portfolios since May after Wacher left to join JANA Investment Advisers.

items.title: Advisers banking on retirees, inheritors for growth but lack strategy
items.teaser: Advisers have named retirees and the next generation of inheritors as their clearest sources of growth over the next five years, yet most practices have not built a distinct investment approach for either group.
items.brief_text: Advisers have named retirees and the next generation of inheritors as their clearest sources of growth over the next five years, yet most practices have not built a distinct investment approach for either group. Based on a survey of 430 Australian advisers, Zenith Investment Partners’ From Adoption to Advantage 2026 report found that three in four [75.3 per cent] rate the growing pool of retirees and pre-retirees as very or extremely important to their practice growth over the next two to five years. Meanwhile, the intergenerational wealth transfer is seeing more than half (57 per cent) say the same of the intergenerational transfer of wealth, as ageing clients pass portfolios to their children. Just 31 per cent of managed account users run a strategy designed specifically for clients in the decumulation phase, even though 90 per cent of practices already have those clients on their books. Getting the order of decisions right for a drawdown client is the kind of sequencing work most practices have not yet formalised and the report found that engagement with the next generation is running far behind. Just 26 per cent of practices have a specific strategy for the adult children who stand to inherit their clients’ portfolios, while 53 per cent are still planning to build one and 21 per cent have no plan to do so. Zenith Investment Partners head of portfolio solutions Andrew Yap said advisers can see exactly where the next five years of growth will come from.

items.title: Housing package estimated to cut 10,700 homes and push rents higher: new modelling
items.teaser: The Master Builders Australia, Housing Industry Association, Property Council of Australia, and the REIA released updated independent modelling of the Federal Budget housing package.
items.brief_text: The Master Builders Australia, Housing Industry Association, Property Council of Australia, and the REIA released updated independent modelling of the Federal Budget housing package. The modelling examines the cumulative impact of the Federal Budget’s primary housing tax reforms, including changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax concession arrangements, together with the $2 billion Housing Support Program. The updated modelling incorporates the additional measure agreed by Labor and the Greens during negotiations to secure passage of the broader package through Parliament that prohibits SMSFs from using LRBAs to purchase ordinary residential investment property. The analysis by Qaive and Tulipwood Economics finds that between 2026–27 and 2029–30, the combined housing measures are estimated to reduce new dwelling starts by 10,700, increase rents by approximately $10 per week, reduce cumulative GDP by approximately $1.05 billion; and cut construction jobs by more than 4,700. The findings represent a further deterioration from the modelling released immediately after the Budget, which already showed that the package would reduce housing construction, weaken economic activity, and place additional pressure on renters. The housing industry bodies said the updated figures reinforce that Australia cannot resolve its housing shortage through policies that make it harder to finance, build, and supply rental homes.

items.title: Australians ‘confused and unconvinced’ by life insurance
items.teaser: Combined research from the Campgemini Research Institute and LIMRA found that 47 per cent of Australian customers who are considering taking out a life insurance policy say they feel apprehensive and that they lack the information needed to make a decision, 5 per cent higher than the global average.
items.brief_text: Combined research from the Campgemini Research Institute and LIMRA found that 47 per cent of Australian customers who are considering taking out a life insurance policy say they feel apprehensive and that they lack the information needed to make a decision, 5 per cent higher than the global average. Younger people were found to be the most wanting of greater clarity, with 54 per cent of 18 to 40-year-olds wanting to buy a policy. Despite this, they were also the most to abandon the process (28 per cent). Overly technical language (37 per cent), affordability concerns (35 per cent), and a perceived lack of relevance to life stage (25 per cent) rank as some of the most common reasons people walk away altogether. The research also found that customers both in Australia and globally are rarely or never contacted after they buy their policy (41 per cent in Australia, 36 per cent globally), with over three quarters saying contact only came when it was time to pay bills and renewals. Notably, the research found that 48 per cent say they’d be more likely to stick with an insurer that is proactive and maintains contact through guidance before, during and after their purchase. However, it appears that a lack of guidance is driving a global uptick in the use of AI to inform decisions, with 51 per cent saying they planned on using the technology in this context.

items.title: Industry funds largest source of rollovers into SMSFs: Class
items.teaser: The 2026 Benchmark Report revealed that between FY23 and FY26, $14.4 billion was rolled into Class SMSFs, around 2.5 times the $5.7 billion rolled out. Industry funds were the largest source of rollover inflows, accounting for 57.2 per cent, while retail funds received 66.7 per cent of rollover outflows.
items.brief_text: The 2026 Benchmark Report revealed that between FY23 and FY26, $14.4 billion was rolled into Class SMSFs, around 2.5 times the $5.7 billion rolled out. Industry funds were the largest source of rollover inflows, accounting for 57.2 per cent, while retail funds received 66.7 per cent of rollover outflows. This data was also backed up by the latest APRA quarterly superannuation report which showed a significant number of rollovers from industry funds into SMSF. Class CEO Tim Steele said flexibility, choice and control are enduring features of SMSFs, with the data clearly demonstrating their important role within a competitive and diverse superannuation system. Steele told SMSF Adviser that given the backdrop of the current regulatory framework, Class wanted to look at the source and destination of funds into and out of SMSFs for the first time. “We had no inkling as to what that data might show us. It could have told a very different story, but it did reinforce some of what you’re seeing from APRA and more broadly in the market, and that is the source of the $14.4 billion of rollovers into SMSFs, at least on the Class system over a four-year period, 57 per cent was industry funds, and that’s really interesting,” he said.

items.title: AI moves into the advice process
items.teaser: Financial advisers could soon spend less time piecing together clients' histories and more time acting on them, as Marloo launches an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that searches entire client books alongside new research showing consumers are increasingly willing to let AI help make financial decisions.
items.brief_text: Financial advisers could soon spend less time piecing together clients' histories and more time acting on them, as Marloo launches an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that searches entire client books alongside new research showing consumers are increasingly willing to let AI help make financial decisions. Marloo co-founder Hardy Michel said using its new Ask Marloo feature can "gain an immediate understanding of clients, including clients they haven't met yet," while receiving updates on activity, potential issues and opportunities. Ask Marloo allows advisers and support staff to query an entire client book and receive answers drawn from meetings, documents, emails and other information held across a business' digital ecosystem. The platform is designed to give advisers a faster view of clients' financial positions, investments insurance, advice history and outstanding tasks. It can also assist advisers taking on acquired or inherited books by providing client overviews without lengthy handover processes. Michel said the technology addresses the industry's reliance on advisers' individual knowledge of clients. "Financial advice currently runs on memory, advisers carry their clients with them, remembering what they said three years ago, what's truly important to them and why they made certain decisions," he said.

items.title: Preparing advice practices for a retiree and inheritance boom
items.teaser: Retirees and inheritors are key growth opportunities for advisers but Zenith notes practices might not be fully optimised to serve their needs yet. Research house Zenith Investment Partners surveyed 430 Australian advisers, in its ‘From Adoption to Advantage 2026’ report.
items.brief_text: Retirees and inheritors are key growth opportunities for advisers but Zenith notes practices might not be fully optimised to serve their needs yet. Research house Zenith Investment Partners surveyed 430 Australian advisers, in its ‘ From Adoption to Advantage 2026 ’ report. The main insights were that 75 per cent of advisers see a growing pool of retiree and pre-retirees as ‘very or extremely important’ as a growth factors in the next two to five years. Another priority identified by 57 per cent of polled advisers was the intergenerational wealth transfer when ageing clients pass portfolios to their children. Andrew Yap, head of portfolio solutions at Zenith, said these figures reaffirm that advisers know where to focus their attention. “Advisers can see exactly where their next five years of growth is coming from. It’s the client in front of them today moving into retirement, and it’s the children who will eventually inherit what’s left,” he said, While their priorities may be clear but Zenith cast doubt over whether advisers are fully prepared for the priorities identified. For example, 90 per cent of practices reporting having decumulation clients on their books but only 31 per cent use a managed account for those clients. This reveals practices can adapt to the identified growth opportunities but that advisers could also become more specialised.

items.title: Something’s wrong when the biggest bill lands with the smallest players
items.teaser: Advice networks are the least “valuable” links in the wealth management chain, yet when something goes wrong they’re too often left to carry the can, even when a failure is not their fault.
items.brief_text: In July I sat in a room with five other advice licensees. Between us, we authorised 936 advisers and accounted for $48.2 billion under advice. We put our actual accounts for last financial year on the wall and added them up. This was not a survey and not a model, but six sets of real numbers. The advice relationships in those six businesses generated $741 million of revenue across the financial services chain. Of that, $416 million went to platforms, investment managers and insurers. That money never appears in an advice business’s accounts. We do not invoice it and we never see it. So, a total of $325 million arrived with the licensees. Of that, $283 million went to the advisers themselves, and $30 million went to operating costs, which is licensing, compliance, technology and professional indemnity. After that, $11 million was left, across six licensees and 936 advisers, for a year’s work. The chart below plots each segment’s valuation multiple against measured risk. Platforms carry the lowest risk and trade at about 95 times earnings; listed advice businesses trade at about 11 times on the same measure; advisory networks carry the highest risk and the lowest multiple. I used to call that pricing revenue rather than risk. I no longer think that is right, or platforms would carry the heaviest rating.

items.title: Asset managers turn to outsourcing, AI: Survey
items.teaser: Global asset managers are sharpening their focus on core capabilities, increasing their use of outsourcing and tightening cost controls as they pursue more disciplined growth, according to a new Northern Trust survey.
items.brief_text: Global asset managers are sharpening their focus on core capabilities, increasing their use of outsourcing and tightening cost controls as they pursue more disciplined growth, according to a new Northern Trust survey. The Driving Growth in Asset Management 2026 report, based on responses from 300 senior executives across North America, Europe, EMEA and Asia-Pacific, found firms are becoming more selective about where they deploy resources amid market volatility, fee pressures and rising operational complexity. Product expansion has fallen as a strategic priority, with 47% of respondents citing it compared with 60% in 2024, while the proportion prioritising product reduction increased from 5% to 28%. "The central theme emerging from our study is a renewed focus on the core: core products, core capabilities, core markets and core client relationships," the report said. The shift towards simplification is also reflected in operating models, with some firms prioritising a major target operating model redesign falling from 75% in 2024 to 46% in 2026. Enhancing quality and accuracy and controlling costs was identified as the leading operational priorities. At the same time, the number of managers planning to outsource non-core activities to achieve their priorities more than doubled to 39% from 18% two years earlier. Northern Trust head of asset managers and private markets for the Americas Ryan Burns said managers were focusing resources on areas where they could differentiate.

items.title: Asset-based fees dwindle as firms price for complexity, not wealth
items.teaser: New research has found that the shift away from asset-based fees is gathering pace, with advice fees increasingly being based on the complexity of the client, not on portfolio size.
items.brief_text: Asset-based fees are losing their grip on financial advice pricing, with the size of a client’s portfolio having significantly less influence on what advisers charge now than it did three years ago, new research has found. Vital Business Partners’ 2026 Advice Fee Benchmarking Report , based on a confidential survey of 143 advice firms representing about 500 advisers and conducted in the first quarter of 2026, finds that pricing now increasingly follows the complexity of a client’s affairs and rewards the adviser’s professional judgement and expertise, not assets under advice. Firms were asked how they price their services generally, and what they would charge to advise five hypothetical clients ranging from a young couple with a mortgage to a high-net-worth family with $12.5 million in assets. The report says the proportion of firms charging a purely asset-based ongoing fee “has fallen from 18 per cent in 2023 to 10 per cent in 2026,” a decline of 8 percentage points, or 44 per cent. The report says fixed fees are now “the most commonly used pricing model for ongoing advice services,” adopted by 49 per cent of firms. Hybrid structures, which combine a fixed fee with a percentage component , have grown fastest of all, more than doubling from 14 per cent of firms in 2023 to 38 per cent in 2026.

items.title: Competence, judgement, diligence the minimum required of licensees
items.teaser: ASIC's finding that former InterPrac boss Garry Crole was neither fit and proper nor competent, and lacked diligence and judgement, is a timely warning: licensee leadership isn't always what advisers assume.
items.brief_text: ASIC’s statement this week that it considered the former chief executive officer and managing director of Sequoia Financial Group – who was also a director and responsible manager of its InterPrac licensee – was neither a fit and proper person nor competent is a timely warning to all advisers that there may be more than meets the eye when it comes to assessing the quality of a licensee’s management. In banning Crole for 10 years from “from performing, as a director or responsible manager, any function involved in carrying on a financial services business”, ASIC said that he “lacked the diligence and judgement required to perform one or more functions as an officer of an entity carrying on a financial services business”. It is a damning assessment of someone carrying out a role that is, frankly, all about diligence, judgement and competence. If you were to sit down and list out the key characteristics of a professional – in any field – those would be at or very close to the top of the list. Maybe you’d add “ethical” to it; ASIC delivered no judgement on that specific issue. Advisers authorised by InterPrac were entitled to expect their licensee’s leadership to be at least fit and proper and competent. Why they didn’t know that it wasn’t is a question only they can answer. Diligence is another issue, and perhaps that was a plus for some InterPrac advisers. But maybe a “light-touch” licensee isn’t all it’s cracked up to be.

items.title: Opposition and peak SMSF body call for a stop to tinkering with rules
items.teaser: Four substantive changes in just five months has led the Shadow Minister for Financial Services Kevin Hogan to call on the government to quit tinkering with the rules. His plea for greater stability and certainty is supported by the peak SMSF industry body.
items.brief_text: The chief executive of the peak self-managed super fund industry body has backed calls by the Shadow Minister for Financial Servies Kevin Hogan for the government to quit tinkering with the rules and provide the sector with greater stability and certainty on how funds are structured, administered and invest. Hogan said in a statement on Thursday that the government has substantively changed the rules for SMSFs four times in just five months. It has introduced the Division 296 tax changes and a higher effective tax rate on the capital gains of super funds that hold their assets indirectly through managed funds such as ETFs, banned SMSFs from borrowing to buy residential property, and last month introduced mandatory trustee education, a written investment strategy, a new ATO veto power over people moving their money into an SMSF, adviser disclosure, and a new CSLR levy contribution. “We don’t know what the education requirement will be, who provides it, or what happens if someone fails. We don’t know in what circumstances the ATO will exercise their new power,” Hogan said. “That’s concerning when the Prime Minister is calling your super a ‘national asset’ to be directed into pet projects like social housing or green energy.” “The 1.2 million Australians with an SMSF don’t want special treatment. They just want stability.

items.title: Finalists announced for the 2026 FAAA Awards
items.teaser: The FAAA has unveiled the finalists for the FAAA annual awards, with the winners set to be announced at this year’s Gala Dinner at the Melbourne Congress on 26 November…
items.brief_text: The FAAA has unveiled the finalists for the FAAA annual awards, with the winners set to be announced at this year’s Gala Dinner at the Melbourne Congress on 26 November 2026. The 2026 FAAA Awards recognise advisers and practices delivering the highest standards of professional advice to Australian consumers. The awards also acknowledge those who go above and beyond, giving back to their communities through pro bono work and volunteering. Additionally, the awards celebrate the next generation of advisers coming through university programs, recognising the emerging talent that will shape the future of the profession. FAAA general manger membership and strategic initiatives, Tania Milnes, says this year’s finalists reflect the breadth of talent across the profession. “The FAAA awards acknowledge those who are truly committed to putting their clients first, supporting their communities, and raising standards across financial advice. “Each finalist embodies the professionalism and care that defines our profession, whether through their exceptional client work, their leadership within their organisations, their contributions to their local community, or their potential as emerging professionals,” Ms Milnes said.

items.title: Fed's rate hike exacerbates Australia's outlook
items.teaser: The Federal Reserve has lifted its interest rate for the first time in more than three years, contributing to the ongoing adversity the global economy is facing, especially in Australia.
items.brief_text: The Federal Reserve has lifted its interest rate for the first time in more than three years, contributing to the ongoing adversity the global economy is facing, especially in Australia. The Fed has called a rate hike overnight, increasing the interest rate by 25 basis points from 3.75% to 4%. Commenting, VanEck head of investments and capital markets Russel Chesler said the move was "widely anticipated", as the renewed surge in oil prices continue to intensify inflation across the global economy. It comes as inflation in the US remains well above the central bank's target rate of 2%, Chesler said, noting oil price surges is also threatening the global economy. "The US economy also remains resilient. August employment increased by 162,000, unemployment is around 4.1%, and consumer and business spending remains reasonably strong," he said. "This data gives the Fed scope to tighten without immediately threatening the labour market. However the more pressing question is whether one rate hike is enough to bring inflation down and if the Fed will need to enter a tightening cycle." Principal Asset Management market strategist Christian Floro agreed, stating the rate increase stemmed from Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh's growing concerns on taming inflation. He is now projecting another hike to come in December.

items.title: What does it mean to choose independence?
items.teaser: Under section 923A of the Corporations Act, use of the terms ‘independent’, ‘impartial’ or ‘unbiased’ in relation to financial advice are tightly restricted.
items.brief_text: Under section 923A of the Corporations Act , use of the terms ‘independent’, ‘impartial’ or ‘unbiased’ in relation to financial advice are tightly restricted. Anyone wanting to use these terms may not accept any commissions for advice or any form of remuneration calculated on the basis of the volume of business placed by the person with an issuer of a financial product, nor can anyone else under their AFSL. Independent advisers also can’t be restricted in what they can recommend meaning they must have an open approved product list (APL), another factor that can make it challenging to exist under a larger licensee while keeping the title. Finally, they can’t have any ownership or ties with product providers such as a super fund or super fund-controlled group as this would ultimately influence the advice being provided by creating a conflict in the service. When considering the hurdles it takes to meet these requirements, commission and risk advice are often the most obvious. Appearing on The ifa Show, independent financial adviser Andrew Saikal-Skea said there are options to deliver risk advice within this model but it can be challenging. “The way that we deal with it is that we only do risk insurance advice as part of comprehensive advice, so we don’t do risk only. But there’s a few ways that it really permeates,” Saikal-Skea said. “Sometimes we’ll have a client come to us. They’ll already have a risk adviser that they work closely with, and that’s great.
